Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

derivations.claim: The coordinate list has $d+d(d-1)/2=m$ entries. Its first $d$ entries recover each diagonal entry of $A$, and each later entry recovers the corresponding symmetric pair by division by $\sqrt2$ from [F3]. Thus it has a unique inverse on $\mathbb R^m$; its coordinate formulas are linear, so $\operatorname{svec}$ is a linear bijection.

For $A,B\in\mathbb S^d$, the Euclidean dot product of their coordinate lists is $\sum_i A_{ii}B_{ii}+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$, because each off-diagonal coordinate contributes $(\sqrt2 A_{ij})(\sqrt2 B_{ij})$. Symmetry gives $\langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_i A_{ii}B_{ii}+\sum_{i<j}(A_{ij}B_{ij}+A_{ji}B_{ji})$, which is the same expression. Hence $\langle\operatorname{svec}(A),\operatorname{svec}(B)\rangle_2=\langle A,B\rangle_F$.

Linearity gives $\operatorname{svec}(A)-\operatorname{svec}(B)=\operatorname{svec}(A-B)$. Applying step 1.2 to $A-B$ with itself and taking the unique nonnegative square roots from [F1]–[F3] yields $\|\operatorname{svec}(A)-\operatorname{svec}(B)\|_2=\|A-B\|_F$. This proves norm preservation.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The assignment

$$T\longmapsto B_T,\qquad B_T(u,v):=\langle Tu,v\rangle,$$

restricts to a bijection between self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V$ and
symmetric bilinear forms on $V$. Under this bijection, non-negative operators
correspond exactly to positive semidefinite forms, and positive operators
correspond exactly to positive definite forms.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an orthogonal eigendecomposition of $A$ and define $A_+$ as in the Statement. It is symmetric and has eigenvalues $\lambda_i^+\ge0$. By [F2] its associated operator is nonnegative, and by [F3] its quadratic form is positive semidefinite; hence $A_+\in\mathbb S_+^d$.

Let $Z\in\mathbb S_+^d$ and set $W=U^TZU$. For each coordinate vector $e_i$, $W_{ii}=e_i^TWe_i=(Ue_i)^TZ(Ue_i)\ge0$; also $W$ is symmetric. Orthogonal invariance [F4] gives $\|A-Z\|_F^2=\|\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)-W\|_F^2$.

Expanding the entry sum [F5], the last square is $\sum_i(\lambda_i-W_{ii})^2+\sum_{i\ne j}W_{ij}^2$. For every $w\ge0$, $(\lambda_i-w)^2\ge(\lambda_i-\lambda_i^+)^2$: if $\lambda_i\ge0$ the right side is zero and equality is attained only at $w=\lambda_i$, while if $\lambda_i<0$ then $w-\lambda_i\ge-\lambda_i$ and equality is attained only at $w=0$. Thus every feasible $Z$ has squared distance at least $\sum_i(\lambda_i-\lambda_i^+)^2$.

For $Z=A_+$ the conjugated matrix $W$ is $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^+,\ldots,\lambda_d^+)$, so all off-diagonal terms vanish and every diagonal term attains its lower bound from step 2.1. Hence $A_+$ is a minimizer.

Equality in the lower bound requires every off-diagonal square in step 2.1 to vanish and every diagonal term to attain its unique scalar minimum. Therefore $W=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^+,\ldots,\lambda_d^+)$ and $Z=U W U^T=A_+$. The minimizer is unique; since the argument applies to any orthogonal eigendecomposition, every allowed decomposition gives this same nearest matrix.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The assignment

$$T\longmapsto B_T,\qquad B_T(u,v):=\langle Tu,v\rangle,$$

restricts to a bijection between self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V$ and
symmetric bilinear forms on $V$. Under this bijection, non-negative operators
correspond exactly to positive semidefinite forms, and positive operators
correspond exactly to positive definite forms.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Then $\operatorname{svec}$ is a linear bijection and preserves inner products and norms; in particular, $\|\operatorname{svec}(A)-\operatorname{svec}(B)\|_2=\|A-B\|_F$ for all $A,B\in\mathbb S^d$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is [[def-equivalent-metrics]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Fix positive integers $d,n,C$, a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,C\}$, and a weight $\mu\in[0,1]$. For each $i$, fix in advance an integer $k_i$ with $0\le k_i\le|\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}|$ and a fixed target-neighbor set $N_i\subseteq\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}$ with $|N_i|=k_i$. These target sets do not change with the matrix being optimized. Let $\mathbb S_+^d$ denote the real symmetric matrices $M$ satisfying $v^TMv\ge0$ for all $v\in\mathbb R^d$, and put $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$. For a real number $z$, let $[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}$. For $M\in\mathbb S_+^d$, define

$$\epsilon_{\rm pull}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}q_M(x_i,x_j),\qquad \epsilon_{\rm push}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le n\\y_l\ne y_i}}[1+q_M(x_i,x_j)-q_M(x_i,x_l)]_+,$$

and $F_\mu(M)=(1-\mu)\epsilon_{\rm pull}(M)+\mu\epsilon_{\rm push}(M)$. This is the fixed-target LMNN training surrogate; it is not a test-error or calibrated/generalization-risk quantity. The quantity $q_M$ is a squared distance, while its square root is the Mahalanobis pseudometric.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

derivations.claim: For each fixed pair $(i,j)$, let $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$. By [F1], $q_M(x_i,x_j)=\operatorname{tr}(MC_{ij})$ is linear in $M$, so every pull term is affine-linear. Each margin expression $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\operatorname{tr}(M(C_{ij}-C_{il}))$ is also affine-linear.

For any affine-linear $h$ and $0\le t\le1$, $h(tM+(1-t)N)=t h(M)+(1-t)h(N)$. The number $t[h(M)]_++(1-t)[h(N)]_+$ is at least $0$ and at least $t h(M)+(1-t)h(N)$, hence it is at least their maximum $[h(tM+(1-t)N)]_+$. Thus each hinge term is convex by [F2].

Finite sums of affine-linear functions and convex hinge functions are convex, and the coefficients $1-\mu$ and $\mu$ are nonnegative because $\mu\in[0,1]$. Applying the convexity inequality term by term proves $F_\mu$ is convex on all symmetric matrices, including the endpoint cases $\mu=0$ and $\mu=1$.

If $M,N\in\mathbb S_+^d$ and $0\le t\le1$, then $tM+(1-t)N$ is symmetric and for every $v$, $v^T(tM+(1-t)N)v=t\,v^TMv+(1-t)\,v^TNv\ge0$. Hence $\mathbb S_+^d$ is convex by [F3]. Restricting the already convex function $F_\mu$ to this convex feasible set yields a convex optimization problem.

where $[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}$. Then $F_\mu$ is convex on the real vector space of symmetric matrices. The feasible set $\mathbb S_+^d=\{M=M^T:v^TMv\ge0\text{ for all }v\in\mathbb R^d\}$ is convex, so minimizing $F_\mu$ over $\mathbb S_+^d$ is a convex optimization problem.

Let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex on a convex set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]), and let $a\in C$. A vector $v$ is a subgradient of $f$ at $a$ when $f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle$ for every $y$ in the domain.

The **subdifferential** is the set

$$\partial f(a):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(a)+\langle v,y-a\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\},$$

with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The definition permits $\partial f(a)$ to be empty or to contain more than one vector.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

derivations.claim: For $a_{ij}=x_i-x_j$, the entrywise inner product satisfies $\langle M,C_{ij}\rangle_F=\sum_{r,s}M_{rs}(a_{ij})_r(a_{ij})_s=a_{ij}^TMa_{ij}=q_M(x_i,x_j)$. Thus each hinge has the form $\phi(M)=\max\{0,1+\langle M,D_{ijl}\rangle_F\}$, with affine argument $h_{ijl}(M)$.

If $h_{ijl}(M)>0$, then $\phi(M)=h_{ijl}(M)$ and $\phi(N)\ge h_{ijl}(N)=\phi(M)+\langle D_{ijl},N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N$. If $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$, then $\phi(M)=0$ and $\phi(N)\ge0=\phi(M)+\langle0,N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N$. Hence $\gamma_{ijl}(M)D_{ijl}$ is a subgradient of this hinge, including the selected zero coefficient at equality.

Each $C_{ij}$ and $D_{ijl}$ is symmetric, so their weighted sum $G(M)$ is symmetric. Each pull term is linear with Frobenius subgradient $C_{ij}$. Adding its supporting equality to the hinge supporting inequalities in step 2.1, weighted by the nonnegative coefficients $1-\mu$ and $\mu$, proves $F_\mu(N)\ge F_\mu(M)+\langle G(M),N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Thus $G(M)$ is a subgradient by [F3].

Since each $\gamma_{ijl}(M)\in\{0,1\}$, the triangle inequality and step 1.2 give $\|G(M)\|_F\le(1-\mu)\sum_{i,j\in N_i}\|C_{ij}\|_F+\mu\sum_{i,j\in N_i,l:y_l\ne y_i}\|D_{ijl}\|_F\le B_{\rm data}$. The bound is finite because the sample and all index sets are finite, and it is independent of $M$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $d,n,C$ be positive integers, let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ be a finite sample with $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,C\}$, let each fixed target set satisfy $N_i\subseteq\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}$, and let $\mu\in[0,1]$. For symmetric $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ write $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$ and define

$$F_\mu(M)=(1-\mu)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}q_M(x_i,x_j)+\mu\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le n\\y_l\ne y_i}}[1+q_M(x_i,x_j)-q_M(x_i,x_l)]_+,$$

where $[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}$. Then $F_\mu$ is convex on the real vector space of symmetric matrices. The feasible set $\mathbb S_+^d=\{M=M^T:v^TMv\ge0\text{ for all }v\in\mathbb R^d\}$ is convex, so minimizing $F_\mu$ over $\mathbb S_+^d$ is a convex optimization problem.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathbb S^d$ be the real symmetric $d\times d$ matrices and let $\mathbb S_+^d=\{M\in\mathbb S^d:v^TMv\ge0\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb R^d\}$. With the Frobenius norm $\|A\|_F=(\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$, the set $\mathbb S_+^d$ is closed in $\mathbb S^d$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathbb S^d$ be the real vector space of symmetric $d\times d$ matrices, and set $m=d(d+1)/2$. Equip $\mathbb S^d$ with the Frobenius inner product $\langle A,B\rangle_F:=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}A_{ij}B_{ij}$ and its induced norm. Define $\operatorname{svec}:\mathbb S^d\to\mathbb R^m$ by listing $A_{11},\ldots,A_{dd}$ first, followed by $\sqrt2 A_{ij}$ for $1\le i<j\le d$ in lexicographic order. Then $\operatorname{svec}$ is a linear bijection and preserves inner products and norms; in particular, $\|\operatorname{svec}(A)-\operatorname{svec}(B)\|_2=\|A-B\|_F$ for all $A,B\in\mathbb S^d$.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb S^d$ be a closed convex set of real symmetric matrices in the Frobenius metric, let $F:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex, let $\operatorname{svec}:\mathbb S^d\to\mathbb R^m$ be the symmetric vectorization isometry, and define $C'=\operatorname{svec}(C)$ and $f:C'\to\mathbb R$ by $f(z)=F(\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(z))$. Then $C'$ is closed and convex and $f$ is convex. If $G$ is a Frobenius subgradient of $F$ at $M\in C$, meaning $F(N)\ge F(M)+\langle G,N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N\in C$, then $\operatorname{svec}(G)$ is a Euclidean subgradient of $f$ at $\operatorname{svec}(M)$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $C\subseteq H$ be nonempty, closed and convex, and let $x\in H$. Then there is exactly one point $p\in C$ with $\|x-p\|=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, that is, a unique nearest point of $C$ to $x$.

Fix the finite labeled sample, fixed target sets, and $\mu\in[0,1]$ of the LMNN objective. For each $j\in N_i$ and each impostor index $l$ with $y_l\ne y_i$, set $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$, $D_{ijl}=C_{ij}-C_{il}$, and $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\langle M,D_{ijl}\rangle_F$, where $\langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{r,s}A_{rs}B_{rs}$. Define $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=1$ if $h_{ijl}(M)>0$ and $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=0$ if $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$. Put

$$G(M)=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}C_{ij}+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\gamma_{ijl}(M)D_{ijl}.$$

For the convex objective $F_\mu$ on $\mathbb S_+^d$, a Frobenius subgradient at $M$ means a symmetric matrix $G$ such that $F_\mu(N)\ge F_\mu(M)+\langle G,N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Then $G(M)$ is a subgradient at every $M\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Moreover, uniformly in $M$,

$$\|G(M)\|_F\le B_{\rm data}:=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\bigl(\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\|x_i-x_l\|_2^2\bigr).$$

At an exact hinge kink $h_{ijl}(M)=0$, the selected subgradient coefficient is $0$.

Finite sums of vectors in $\mathbb R^n$ use the additive finite-list sum of [[def-linear-combination-and-span]]; sums of real coefficients use [[def-finite-sum]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex. The finite-budget projected subgradient procedure takes $x_0\in C$, an integer budget $N\ge1$, and positive stepsizes $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{N-1}$. At iteration $k$, an oracle returns either failure or a pair $(f(x_k),g_k)$ with $g_k\in\partial f(x_k)$, where subgradient has the meaning in [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]. On a valid response set
$$x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha_k g_k),$$
where $P_C(u)$ is the unique nearest point in $C$ to $u$. On an oracle failure at iteration $k$, return status **oracle-failure**, the feasible current iterate, the completed update count, and the least-index best among values observed so far if any (otherwise report none); a full-horizon average is not returned. If all $N$ calls succeed, return status **budget-exhausted**, the final iterate, the weighted average $\bar x_N=(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k)/(\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k)$, and a least-index minimizer of observed values among $x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1}$. Report status and completed update count. This finite procedure makes no convergence claim.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, let $f:C\to\mathbb R$ be convex, and run [[alg-projected-subgradient-method]] for $N\ge1$ steps with positive $\alpha_k$. Assume all $N$ oracle calls return valid pairs. Suppose a global minimizer $x^*\in C$ exists and the oracle vectors obey $\|g_k\|_2\le G$; let $R\ge\|x_0-x^*\|_2$. Set $A_N=\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k>0$ and $\bar x_N=A_N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}\alpha_kx_k$. Then
$$\max\left\{\min_{0\le k<N}\bigl(f(x_k)-f(x^*)\bigr),\ f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\right\}\le\frac{R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2}{2A_N}.$$

Let $d\ge1$ and let $A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric. There exists an orthogonal eigendecomposition $A=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^T$. For any such decomposition define $\lambda_i^+=\max\{\lambda_i,0\}$ and $A_+=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^+,\ldots,\lambda_d^+)U^T$. Let $\mathbb S_+^d$ be the set of real symmetric matrices $Z$ with $v^TZv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\|B\|_F=(\sum_{i,j}B_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. Then $A_+$ is the unique minimizer of $\|A-Z\|_F$ over $Z\in\mathbb S_+^d$, so its value is independent of the chosen orthogonal eigendecomposition.

The cone contains $0$; [F1] makes it convex, [F2] makes it closed in Frobenius distance, and [F3] transfers both properties to $C'$. By [F4], $\mathbb R^m$ is a real Hilbert space; under [A1], [F5] gives a unique Euclidean projection onto $C'$, which is the projection used in [F7]. The explicit matrix update is that projection because [F9] identifies the unique Frobenius-nearest PSD matrix.

For every $t<T$, the displayed data formula in [F6] computes $G(M_t)$ and its bound. The point $M^*$ maps to a global minimizer $z^*=\operatorname{svec}(M^*)$ of $f$ on $C'$, the initial point satisfies $\|z_0-z^*\|_2=R$, and the positive step sizes give $A_T>0$. By linearity of $\operatorname{svec}^{-1}$, the Euclidean weighted average maps to $\overline M_T$ as defined in the Statement. Each iterate lies in $\mathbb S_+^d$, so convexity [F1] puts $\overline M_T$ there; bijectivity also preserves the finite-list minimum, so the Euclidean bound from step 1.3 is exactly the displayed matrix bound.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A real matrix $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is positive semidefinite, written $M\succeq0$, when it is symmetric and $v^{T}Mv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^d$. For $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$, define the squared Mahalanobis distance and its nonnegative square root by

$$q_M(x,x') := (x-x')^{T}M(x-x'),\qquad d_M(x,x') := \sqrt{q_M(x,x')}.$$

The square root is defined because $q_M(x,x')\ge0$. A pseudometric is a nonnegative symmetric function that vanishes on the diagonal and satisfies the triangle inequality, but may assign distance zero to distinct points. The function $d_M$ is called the Mahalanobis pseudometric associated with $M$; $q_M=d_M^2$ is its squared-distance form. The theorem on this page proves the pseudometric properties and the equivalent linear-feature representation.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be real symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning $v^TMv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^d$. Define $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$ and $d_M(x,x')=\sqrt{q_M(x,x')}$. Then there is a real matrix $L\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $M=L^TL$ and, for all $x,x'\in\mathbb R^d$, $d_M(x,x')=\|Lx-Lx'\|_2$. Consequently $d_M$ is nonnegative, symmetric, zero on the diagonal, and satisfies the triangle inequality, without asserting separation of distinct points.

Fix positive integers $d,n,C$, a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,C\}$, and a weight $\mu\in[0,1]$. For each $i$, fix in advance an integer $k_i$ with $0\le k_i\le|\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}|$ and a fixed target-neighbor set $N_i\subseteq\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}$ with $|N_i|=k_i$. These target sets do not change with the matrix being optimized. Let $\mathbb S_+^d$ denote the real symmetric matrices $M$ satisfying $v^TMv\ge0$ for all $v\in\mathbb R^d$, and put $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$. For a real number $z$, let $[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}$. For $M\in\mathbb S_+^d$, define

$$\epsilon_{\rm pull}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}q_M(x_i,x_j),\qquad \epsilon_{\rm push}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le n\\y_l\ne y_i}}[1+q_M(x_i,x_j)-q_M(x_i,x_l)]_+,$$

Fix positive integers $d,n,C$, a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n}$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,C\}$, and a weight $\mu\in[0,1]$. For each $i$, fix in advance an integer $k_i$ with $0\le k_i\le|\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}|$ and a fixed target-neighbor set $N_i\subseteq\{j\ne i:y_j=y_i\}$ with $|N_i|=k_i$. These target sets do not change with the matrix being optimized. Let $\mathbb S_+^d$ denote the real symmetric matrices $M$ satisfying $v^TMv\ge0$ for all $v\in\mathbb R^d$, and put $q_M(x,x')=(x-x')^TM(x-x')$. For a real number $z$, let $[z]_+=\max\{z,0\}$. For $M\in\mathbb S_+^d$, define

$$\epsilon_{\rm pull}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}q_M(x_i,x_j),\qquad \epsilon_{\rm push}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le n\\y_l\ne y_i}}[1+q_M(x_i,x_j)-q_M(x_i,x_l)]_+,$$

and $F_\mu(M)=(1-\mu)\epsilon_{\rm pull}(M)+\mu\epsilon_{\rm push}(M)$. This is the fixed-target LMNN training surrogate; it is not a test-error or calibrated/generalization-risk quantity. The quantity $q_M$ is a squared distance, while its square root is the Mahalanobis pseudometric.

Fix the finite labeled sample, fixed target sets, and $\mu\in[0,1]$ of the LMNN objective. For each $j\in N_i$ and each impostor index $l$ with $y_l\ne y_i$, set $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$, $D_{ijl}=C_{ij}-C_{il}$, and $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\langle M,D_{ijl}\rangle_F$, where $\langle A,B\rangle_F=\sum_{r,s}A_{rs}B_{rs}$. Define $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=1$ if $h_{ijl}(M)>0$ and $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=0$ if $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$. Put

$$G(M)=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}C_{ij}+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\gamma_{ijl}(M)D_{ijl}.$$

For the convex objective $F_\mu$ on $\mathbb S_+^d$, a Frobenius subgradient at $M$ means a symmetric matrix $G$ such that $F_\mu(N)\ge F_\mu(M)+\langle G,N-M\rangle_F$ for every $N\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Then $G(M)$ is a subgradient at every $M\in\mathbb S_+^d$. Moreover, uniformly in $M$,

$$\|G(M)\|_F\le B_{\rm data}:=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\bigl(\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2+\|x_i-x_l\|_2^2\bigr).$$

At an exact hinge kink $h_{ijl}(M)=0$, the selected subgradient coefficient is $0$.

Use the finite sample, fixed target sets, weight $\mu\in[0,1]$, and objective $F_\mu$ defined by the LMNN objective item. The inputs are an integer budget $T\ge1$, an initial matrix $M_0\in\mathbb S_+^d$, and positive step sizes $\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_{T-1}$. Let $m=d(d+1)/2$ and use $\operatorname{svec}:\mathbb S^d\to\mathbb R^m$, the linear isometry that lists the diagonal entries followed by the $\sqrt2$-scaled upper-triangle entries in lexicographic order. Set $C'=\operatorname{svec}(\mathbb S_+^d)$ and $f(z)=F_\mu(\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(z))$; this is a nonempty closed convex domain and $f$ is convex.

Initialize $z_0=\operatorname{svec}(M_0)$. At each $t=0,\ldots,T-1$, put $M_t=\operatorname{svec}^{-1}(z_t)$ and compute the Frobenius subgradient

$$G_t=(1-\mu)\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}C_{ij}+\mu\sum_i\sum_{j\in N_i}\sum_{l:y_l\ne y_i}\gamma_{ijl}(M_t)(C_{ij}-C_{il}),$$

where $C_{ij}=(x_i-x_j)(x_i-x_j)^T$, $h_{ijl}(M)=1+\langle M,C_{ij}-C_{il}\rangle_F$, $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=1$ when $h_{ijl}(M)>0$, and $\gamma_{ijl}(M)=0$ when $h_{ijl}(M)\le0$. It updates $z_{t+1}=P_{C'}(z_t-\eta_t\operatorname{svec}(G_t))$, where $P_{C'}$ is the unique nearest point in the Euclidean norm. Equivalently, form $A_t=M_t-\eta_tG_t$, choose an orthogonal eigendecomposition $A_t=U_t\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{t,1},\ldots,\lambda_{t,d})U_t^T$, and set

$$M_{t+1}=U_t\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\max\{\lambda_{t,1},0\},\ldots,\max\{\lambda_{t,d},0\}\bigr)U_t^T.$$

All $T$ oracle calls succeed; the generic method reports budget-exhausted after $T$ updates. The requested final iterate is $M_T$; its status, completed update count, weighted average, and least-index best observed iterate are also defined by the generic method. This finite procedure makes no unconditional convergence, optimality, empirical-error, or generalization claim.
